extraction.name: MATH (Mathematics Aptitude Test of Heuristics)
extraction.description: A dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems (7,500 training, 5,000 test) spanning seven subjects and tagged by difficulty from 1 to 5. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution formatted in LaTeX and Asymptote, paired with a final boxed answer for exact-match evaluation, designed to measure mathematical problem-solving ability in machine learning models.
extraction.creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Problems for the MATH dataset were sourced from high school math competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME, collected from Art of Problem Solving (aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests). The paper also introduces the auxiliary AMPS dataset, collected by pulling over 100,000 problems from Khan Academy (via github.com/Khan/khan-exercises/) and generating approximately 5 million problems via 100 hand-designed Mathematica scripts.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Competitions from the Mathematical Association of America (MAA) and Art of Problem Solving (AoPS) community archives; Khan Academy exercises; algorithmic generation scripts using Mathematica's computer algebra system.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions were formatted using LaTeX and Asymptote vector graphics language. Final answers were enclosed within a \boxed{} command. Strict normalization and formatting rules were applied to ensure unique ground truth answers: simplifying probability fractions, standardizing fraction notation (x/y for matrices, \frac{x}{y} otherwise), omitting multiplication signs in coefficients, ordering multi-variable expressions alphabetically and polynomials by decreasing degree, and establishing equivalence rules for fraction forms, parentheses styles, spacing, and factor permutations.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Difficulty levels (from 1 to 5) and subject categorizations follow the Art of Problem Solving (AoPS) classification. Step-by-step solutions and final boxed answers were curated alongside competition problems or generated by scripts.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: For the rough human-level comparison benchmark, six university students studying computer science participated: four authors of the paper, and two acquaintances (including a three-time IMO gold medalist and an AMC 10 perfect scorer).
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: High model performance on mathematical problem-solving could have ramifications for cheating on homework and mathematics exams. The authors specify they do not intend for the dataset to train models to help students cheat, but rather to forecast reasoning capabilities.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Current large language models achieve low accuracy (3.0% to 6.9%) and show slow scaling trends. Generating intermediate step-by-step solutions currently degrades model test accuracy due to error cascading/snowballing. Models are overconfident (error detection AUROC is low at 68.8%). Performance declines substantially on Level 5 problems.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving and multi-step reasoning capabilities in machine learning models; pretraining on mathematical fundamentals (via AMPS); fine-tuning models to generate step-by-step derivations and explanations. Not intended for facilitating student cheating on mathematics coursework.
